grief.title: My Grief Map
grief.intro: Use the parts that fit today. You do not have to finish the map or make the loss meaningful.
map: What is different in daily life?
Person, relationship, role, place, future, or part of life
Memory, story, ritual, object, prayer, song, place
support: Who can I be honest with?
What do I need help carrying?
What do I want others to know?
grief.note: If safety or basic care is becoming difficult, bring that concern to a clinician. This map is a conversation aid, not a safety assessment.
grief.companion_intro: Ask which part of the map the person wants to talk about. Leave space for mixed feelings, silence, and ordinary life.
helper_points: Use the person's own words. Do not require a positive meaning or a particular grief stage.
Offer practical help and company in the form the person wants.
Ask about changes in daily functioning and safety when concerns arise; use a fuller assessment when needed.
planning: A time or situation that feels hard
Something I want to keep close
Something I do not want pushed
review: What gave me a little more room?
What should we check or change next time?
related: Making Room for Grief · short guide
sources: NHS: grief after bereavement or loss

care.title: My Personal Care Plan
care.intro: Choose one routine. Find what makes it hard, then try a support you want.
setup: What do I want to make easier?
success: How I will know it helps
care.note: If care suddenly gets much harder, check health, pain, mood, sleep, and access with the right professional. Do not assume it is only a habit problem.
care.companion_intro: Plan around the person's priorities, access needs, and choice. Success may mean less effort or more control over the routine.
helper_points: Watch where the routine gets stuck. Offer one change at a time.
Ask before helping, touching, or changing products. Keep the person's privacy and choices central.
Keep helpful access supports available. Consider medical or occupational-therapy input for pain, motor demands, or persistent difficulty.
planning: What can be ready in advance?
What my helper and I agree to do
review: What was easier or more under my control?
What will we keep, change, or check next?
related: When Hygiene Tasks Are Hard · short guide
sources: National Autistic Society: sensory processing and support

reset.title: My After-School Reset Plan
reset.intro: Home is where I get to land. Choose what helps before adding the next demand.
groups: I can show what I need
signals: tight, fast, heavy, hot, shaky, numb
cry, hide, pace, freeze, shut down
reset.note: For adults: offer choices without making this a quiz. Plan during a calm time. The child can tell or show when they have more room; address immediate safety needs calmly.
reset.companion_title: Plan the landing before school ends
reset.companion_intro: Notice patterns across school, travel, and home. A reset is support, not something a child must earn.
helper_points: Offer time, space, and a manageable way to communicate after overload.
Ask which choices help. Keep touch, noise, and talking within what the child can manage.
Share useful observations with school or a clinician when needed. This plan does not explain every cause of distress.
planning: What used up room at school or on the way home?
How I show I am ready
One manageable next step we agree on
review: What helped the landing or recovery?
What should we change or watch next?
related: After School Is a Landing, Not a Launch · short guide
sources: National Autistic Society: responding to overload
National Autistic Society: sensory processing and support
